p.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network

ext.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network
ext.venue: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2503.11745 [physics.soc-ph]. No journal publication is stated in the text.
ext.document_type: Empirical network-science preprint (main text pp. 1-9, references, Supplementary Information pp. 1-50). Introduces the LobbyView database and analyzes it.
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 5,280 lines of the text file (172,891 chars), covering main text pp. 1-9, references, and SI Sections I-XIV (pp. 1-50), in six chunks. The text is OCR-style extraction with ligature errors, so quoted wording is approximate. Annotation file read in full: 217 items, all Highlights by Paul Goff, zero sticky notes, zero comments, no subjects. Annotation page numbers match printed page numbers. Paul's covered text is not reproduced verbatim (copyright limit on source text); each highlight is summarized by topic and can be located by page and index in the annotation JSON at C:/Users/pgoff/Documents/research/_annots/a0c3322fb2cd.json.
ext.research_question: How does the US federal lobbying network (clients, registrants, lobbyists, government entities, legislators) evolve over time? Specifically: (a) what growth and attachment rules govern client-registrant ties; (b) how does the network adapt to crises and to election or administration cycles; (c) can LDA disclosure data support probabilistic analysis of lobbying pathways for individual bills, issues, or firms, demonstrated on the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA, 2011).
ext.theory: Network science and statistical physics rather than a formal political-economy model. Preferential attachment and cumulative advantage (Barabasi-Albert; Price's Matthew effect) explain hierarchy in K-Street registrant client counts. Attachment and detachment are treated as countervailing forces that stabilize the network. A five-layer directed multipartite graph is used. The political business cycle (Nordhaus 1975) is the framing for election-synchronized targeting. Partisan polarization is measured with cosponsorship and co-association bipartisan indices.
ext.identification: None causal. The analysis is descriptive. Event-timing associations (2007-08 financial crisis, HLOGA 2007, 9/11, COVID-19, presidential terms) are shown as overlays without a counterfactual or instrument. Null comparisons use a bipartite configuration model for clustering and component size (SI IX). The SOPA result is a single case study using conditional probability shifts against a baseline (main p. 8). The paper's own wording is 'supporting the hypothesis' and 'lobbying is strategic'.
ext.data: LobbyView relational database built from LDA LD-2 quarterly/semiannual filings. Period 1999-2023. Analyzed sample: 1,277,411 filings (SI Fig S2). Full LobbyView holds more than 1.6 million reports covering about 87 billion USD (main p. 2; SI Fig S4 gives 87.5 billion). Unit of observation: the filing, aggregated into one directed multilayer network per year. Layers: clients, registrants (K-Street external firms and In-House departments), lobbyists, government entities (agencies and chambers), legislators (members of Congress). Example snapshot 2017 (Fig 1B): 10,694 clients, 4,405 registrants, 11,543 lobbyists, 128 government entities, 374 legislators. Industry sectors use NAICS 2-digit codes (20 sectors) via S&P Compustat, covering about 40% of clients. Issues: 79 LDA issue codes; bills extracted by regex. Legislator data: US Digital Service congressional database. External linkage: Compustat, BoardEx, Orbis, NOMINATE. SOPA case: 67 publicly traded firms lobbying in Q4 2011 (main Fig 4 caption).
ext.method: Descriptive and empirical statistics on a time-indexed multilayer directed graph. Steps: (1) in- and out-degree CCDFs by layer; MLE fits of an augmented power law with exponential cutoff, a log-normal and a Weibull, with the power law preferred (Fig 2F, SI Fig S11). (2) Preferential attachment: attachment and detachment functions by registrant in-degree, cumulated, with linearity tested (Fig 2E, SI VIII.B). (3) Survival or retention probability by year and age-conditioned exit (SI VIII.A). (4) Pareto charts and Gini indices of monetary flow (SI V). (5) Issue and target portfolios: client-share matrices, year-to-year Spearman correlation, PCA (SI XI). (6) Bipartite clustering coefficients and largest connected component, against a configuration-model null (SI IX). (7) SOPA pathway probabilities: uniform client draw, conditional probability shift Delta P(sector | SOPA) (Fig 4, SI XII). (8) Polarization: bipartisan cosponsorship index, lobbyist bipartisan index, modularity (SI XIII).
ext.scope: US federal lobbying disclosed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) of 1995 as amended by HLOGA 2007, years 1999-2023. Population is registrants, clients and lobbyists in LD-2 filings. Excludes informal or unreported advocacy (stated scope condition, SI I.C), PAC and donation channels (only mentioned), LD-203 contribution reports, 'no activity' filings, and superseded filings. Institutions covered: Congress (legislators and committees) and federal agencies and departments.

key_findings.finding: Annual churn of K-Street registrants: 200-500 new registrants enter each year, with a comparable number exiting.
Long-run turnover: of the registrants active in 2000, only a minority remain active in 2020.
key_findings.location: main text p. 5 (cites Fig 2C; survival curve is labeled Fig 2D in caption)

key_findings.finding: Client-registrant rewiring is large: a substantial share of clientship ties is replaced every year.
key_findings.numbers: up to one-third of clientship connections each year

key_findings.finding: Linear preferential attachment: the chance a new client selects a registrant is proportional to that registrant's current client count. Attachment and detachment are both linear in degree and act as countervailing forces.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 4-5 (Fig 2E); SI VIII.B (Fig S27)
key_findings.numbers: cumulative attachment function ~ c^2; quadratic functional form

key_findings.finding: Heavy-tailed clients-per-K-Street-registrant distribution: a small elite dominates the lobbying market.
key_findings.location: main text p. 5 (Fig 2F caption p. 4); SI IV.B (Fig S11)
key_findings.numbers: power-law exponent d = 1.46 (caption) / about 1.5 (text) / 1.54 (SI); cutoff c0 = 86 (caption) / about 85 (text) / 86 (SI)
about 80% of K-Street income from 20% of registrants

key_findings.finding: Global layer-to-layer degree distributions were stable across 25 years despite high member churn.
Short-term decline in active K-Street firms after 2009, persisting for much of the following decade. Causes are offered as plausible (2007-08 crisis; HLOGA 2007 revolving-door limits) but not tested.
key_findings.numbers: decline after 2009 (no magnitude stated in text)

key_findings.finding: Issue portfolios respond to crises: spikes in disaster-planning and small-business lobbying in early COVID-19; portfolio rearrangement after 9/11 and during COVID-19.
key_findings.numbers: no numeric values given in text

key_findings.finding: Target (agency) portfolios are block-diagonal across presidential terms; lobbyists keep approaching the same agencies within an administration but adapt quickly on leadership change. Some agencies such as the National Economic Council follow the presidential election cycle.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 5-6; Fig 3F; SI XI (Figs S34-S38)
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; PCA: e1 explains more than 48% (text) or 38% (caption) of variance; e2 explains 13%

key_findings.finding: SOPA 2011: IT-sector firms were far more represented among SOPA lobbyists than in the general client base, and IT firms hired multiple K-Street firms, approached the Executive Office of the President more often, and assembled bipartisan lobbying teams more often.
key_findings.location: main text p. 8; Fig 4 (inset Fig 4B; panels C-E); SI XII
key_findings.numbers: P(IT | SOPA) > 0.4 vs P(IT) about 0.1 (shift about +0.3, derived from the stated values); no numeric values stated for panels C-E

key_findings.finding: Monetary concentration of lobbying is persistently high; lobbyist income concentration is lower but above US income Gini.
key_findings.numbers: cumulative Gini about 0.8 for clients and K-Street registrants over 2 decades; about 0.6 for lobbyists; US income Gini about 0.4 (World Bank, as cited)

key_findings.finding: Registrant-lobbyist contracts are hierarchical at the firm level but egalitarian at the individual lobbyist level.
key_findings.location: SI V.A (Fig S17); SI IV.B (Fig S12C-D); pp. 16, 19
key_findings.numbers: 20% of K-Street registrants hold more than 70% of lobbyist contracts; about 90% of lobbyists have no documented government or legislator association

key_findings.finding: Exit probability of lobbying actors falls with age, with a shared timescale of about 10 years across clients, registrants and lobbyists.
Network-structure checks: clustering coefficients of bipartite projections match the configuration-model null. Only the client-K-Street subgraph has a giant connected component at all times.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative match; no numeric values in text

key_findings.finding: Registrant income is high when a registrant reaches government or legislator associations; each association type alone is sufficient for high income.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; income in USD by association count

key_findings.finding: Polarization contrast: Senate cosponsorship across parties fell sharply, while lobbying shows no matching trend. Bipartisan lobbying teams earn more income per lobbyist.
key_findings.location: SI XIII (Fig S46); pp. 48-50; main text p. 8 (Fig 4D)
key_findings.numbers: Senate bipartisan cosponsorship down about 40% over 25 years; lobbyist bipartisan index not decreasing; lobbyist modularity near zero

key_findings.finding: Legislator-lobbyist ties via past employment are common but incomplete.
key_findings.location: main text pp. 2-3; SI III (Fig S9); p. 10
key_findings.numbers: 20% of lobbyists had a known government connection in 2023; main text says 80% of Senators and 60% of Representatives have at least one active connected lobbyist, while SI III says about 80% and 50% (inconsistent)

limitations: Revolving-door and legislator ties are inferred only from past-employment disclosures. Lobbyists do not give timelines for covered positions, so recency cannot be established (SI I.D).
Direct registrant-legislator contacts are not required by the LDA and are not observed.

The client-registrant-lobbyist layered graph is a first-order approximation that obscures polyadic interactions; higher-order and multilayer structure is deferred to future work (main pp. 2-3; SI VI; Discussion p. 8).

Entity resolution is imperfect. Client matching uses search-assisted disambiguation, which the paper says fails for long-defunct firms and non-public-facing firms, and resolves to third-party directories (SI I.C fn. 2). Lobbyist name resolution is score-based and uncertain.
Low-cost filings are assigned a reporting-threshold value as an upper bound, a heuristic the paper says is immaterial to results (SI I.C).
Filings for 1999-2007 were on paper and needed OCR, and the 2008 switch from semiannual to quarterly filing doubled report counts; the paper aggregates to annual data.
Only about 40% of clients can be mapped to NAICS sectors via Compustat, so sector-level results cover public or Compustat-linked firms only (SI XII.A).
The SOPA analysis is a single bill, a single quarter, and a restricted subsample; the paper says subsampling can bias results (SI V).

The paper states that fitting a network-evolution model to the lobbying network is beyond its scope (SI VIII). Its preferential-attachment interpretation is descriptive and does not test competing mechanisms.
Polarization analysis is described by the authors as exploratory (SI XIII).

Reported numbers conflict across the text: power-law exponent (1.46 / 1.5 / 1.54); PCA variance (48% vs 38%); legislator connection shares (60% vs 50% for Representatives); survival-curve panel (Fig 2C vs 2D); filing count (1.6 million vs 1,277,411 analyzed).
Anonymized relational data and code are on OSF (osf.io/y2hnm); full identifiers and some fields require contacting the authors (SI XIV).

rel.summary_md:
Bacik, Ondras, Rudkin, Dunkel and Kim build a yearly five-layer directed network from LobbyView, which is derived from LDA LD-2 filings. The layers are clients, registrants (K-Street firms and in-house departments), lobbyists, government entities and legislators. The analyzed sample is 1,277,411 filings from 1999 to 2023. The work is descriptive network physics, not causal inference. Its main findings: 200-500 K-Street registrants enter and leave each year, and only 20% of the firms active in 2000 were still active in 2020. Up to one-third of client-registrant ties are rewired each year. Attachment is linearly preferential, which gives a heavy-tailed distribution of clients per firm (exponent about 1.5, cutoff about 86). Money is concentrated: the cumulative Gini is about 0.8 for clients and firms. Agency-target portfolios form blocks by presidential administration. Senate cross-party cosponsorship fell about 40% while lobbyist bipartisanship did not fall. A single SOPA case (Q4 2011, 67 public firms) shows the IT sector over-represented, with P(IT | SOPA) above 0.4 against a base rate of about 0.1.

For Paul's systems the paper matters mostly through what LDA data cannot show. Legislators enter the paper's network only through lobbyists' one-time disclosures of past covered positions. Those disclosures have no dates, and the LDA never records registrant-legislator contact. That independently supports the system's refutation of the lobbied-member link and its fail-closed handling of contacts and identities. The paper's 40% NAICS coverage supports the rule that client names decide classification. Its K-Street versus in-house distinction supports Mentat's rule of never adding hired-firm and in-house lobbying. Its "election synchronization" finding is about which agencies are targeted, not about money, so it does not support a phase effect on lobbying dollars. The paper contains no press or sentiment data.

bearings.paper_claim: The LDA does not require reporting of direct registrant-legislator contacts, and the paper does not observe them. Legislators enter the network only through a lobbyist's disclosed past covered position: 'legislator inclusion via active lobbyist'. About 90% of lobbyists have no documented government or legislator association, and 20% had a known government connection in 2023.
bearings.paper_location: main pp. 2-3; SI I.D (pp. 20-21); SI III (Fig S9); SI IV.B (Fig S12C-D); SI p. 23
bearings.system_side: The member-year network credits every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill. That makes P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so the link is REFUTED as evidence of influence. The interaction ledger states that the LD-2 form has no position field and has no member field.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence carries over fully because it describes the same federal LD-2 form. The paper uses the same data and states plainly that legislator contact is unobserved, so nothing in LD-2 can rescue the bill-roster join. An independent contact measure is still required. The paper's own legislator edges come from revolving-door disclosure, so they are not contact evidence either, and influence language is barred on them.

bearings.paper_claim: Only about 40% of clients map to NAICS sectors through Compustat, so the paper's sector results cover Compustat-linked firms only. Client disambiguation is search-assisted and the paper says it fails for long-defunct firms and firms that do not face the public. The analysis window runs 1999-2023, with issue-portfolio plots across those years.
bearings.paper_location: SI XII.A (p. 55); SI I.C fn. 2 (p. 18); SI Fig S2; main Fig 3A-B
bearings.system_side: Client names decide classification and NAICS is only suggestive. High confidence requires a name rule. In the 2024-10-25 bulk-export vintage, issue-code coverage collapses after filing_year 2021.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 40% figure is for all LobbyView clients and the share for finance clients is not reported. It still supports not relying on NAICS for credit-union versus bank classification. The paper plots issue portfolios through 2023, which suggests the post-2021 collapse comes from the bulk-export vintage rather than LobbyView's internal tables. That is UNVERIFIED and should be checked against the OSF release before anyone assumes newer coverage exists.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper defines a government-association function g(l,y), which is monotone in year, and a political-association function p(l,y), which is not monotone. Both are built from one-time disclosures of covered positions, and lobbyists give no timelines for those positions, so recency cannot be established.
bearings.system_side: Activity descriptions are matched to members using gold positives that name the member. Negatives come from the same organization's roster join. Paul's design memos borrow only documented definitions from the LobbyView lineage.
bearings.code_ref: component lists no code path (lane path not recorded); nearest shipped surface: fec/lobbying/lobby_interactions.py:19-24 (position_basis='not_disclosed')
bearings.transfer_conditions: The g and p definitions can be reused as documented, timestamp-free association labels. They are not contact evidence and must not become edge weights (D-021). Any use needs a 'no timeline' label, because the paper itself says it cannot date the ties.

bearings.paper_claim: Covered-position disclosures are made once and have no dates, so recency cannot be established. Co-listing on filings shows registrant-lobbyist contracts, not dated co-work.
bearings.paper_location: SI I.D (pp. 20-21); SI p. 22 (registrant-lobbyist contract edge definition)
bearings.system_side: Filing-year-only episodes are routed separately as 'co_reported_firm_association'. They carry temporal_status 'filing_year_association_only' and weak=True, and are reachable only when include_weak is set (default False, filing_cost 5 >= historical_cost 3). Dated Politico co-work stays the main tie source.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper describes federal LDA lobbyists, and the routes cover congressional staff. The paper's point that filing data cannot date relationships applies directly to the filing-year hops. It says nothing about the dated payroll-overlap hops. Routes are heuristic introduction paths, not access probabilities (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Registrants split into K-Street firms that file for others and in-house self-filers. The monetary field differs between them (income for firms, expenses for self-filers), and self-filers have a higher reporting threshold.
bearings.paper_location: SI p. 17 (self-filer flag, monetary field and threshold); SI p. 19 (formal registrant-type definitions)
bearings.system_side: The lobbying card shows hired_firms (income_total) and in_house (expenses_total) side by side and never adds them.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is the same LD-2 accounting, so the evidence carries over fully. The paper also assigns low-cost reports a threshold value as an upper bound. If Mentat's sector_spend rows ever take values from LobbyView, check whether they include that imputation.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's election-cycle 'synchronization' refers to target portfolios: agency-approach correlations form blocks by presidential administration, and some agencies such as the National Economic Council follow the presidential cycle. It reports no effect of election phase on lobbying dollars, and it aggregates data annually.
bearings.paper_location: main pp. 5-6; Fig 3F; SI XI (Figs S34-S38); SI p. 16 (annualization)
bearings.system_side: The live refit models giving and lobbying measures as log models of presidential versus midterm phase plus trajectory. The seasonal-naive baseline repeats the same-phase cycle from four years earlier.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports a four-year, administration-linked periodicity in whom lobbyists target, not in how much they spend. It cannot justify a phase coefficient on lobbying dollars, which has to rest on Mentat's own backtests. The PAC side (D-092) is not addressed at all, because the paper excludes PAC channels.

bearings.paper_claim: The Senate bipartisan cosponsorship index fell about 40% over 1999-2023 and the House index also fell. Lobbyist bipartisan share did not fall, and lobbyist modularity is near zero.
bearings.system_side: bpf is a static per-member cross-party cosponsorship share with a default of 0.24 for missing members. It feeds cpf_diffusion and other parts of the kernel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's index is a chamber-level aggregate, not a member-level trait. It shows the cross-party baseline is strongly era-dependent, so a bpf or default fixed in one window should not be carried across Congresses without naming the window. It does not validate bpf as a measure of bridging.

bearings.paper_claim: LobbyView's lobbyist name disambiguation is score-based and uncertain. Client matching relies on search-assisted lookup that resolves to third-party directories and fails for defunct firms.
bearings.paper_location: SI I.C fn. 2 (p. 18); SI p. 20 (lobbyist disambiguation)
bearings.system_side: A never-guess ladder plus payroll-evidence pins, with record-pair titles and organization strings required to be at least 8 characters.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The domains differ: LDA lobbyist names versus congressional payroll staff. Wherever LobbyView lobbyist IDs enter the staffer graph as identities (D-021 allows identity use), treat them as probabilistic merges, not ground truth. The system's ladder is stricter than LobbyView's.

gaps_exposed: The system has no government-entity (agency or chamber) layer from LD-2. Lobbying links reach Congress only through bill citations. The paper shows agency targeting shifts by administration, and that executive-branch targeting (EOP) separated the IT firms on SOPA.

Lobbying relationships are not treated as time-varying. Up to one-third of client-registrant ties rewire each year and about 20% of registrants survive two decades, so any static organization-to-firm or firm-to-lobbyist mapping goes stale within a year.

There is no configuration-model null for the staffer or cosponsor graphs. The paper tests clustering and giant components against a bipartite configuration model, which would directly test whether staffer degree is container size (r = 0.87 recorded).
Whether the bulk export's post-2021 issue-code collapse is a vintage artifact is unchecked. The paper plots issue portfolios through 2023 and points to OSF data (osf.io/y2hnm). This is UNVERIFIED.
The low-cost-report upper-bound imputation and the 2008 change from semiannual to quarterly filing are not documented as checks in Melange's or Mentat's LDA level series.
flags: Paul's press-pillar and press-value-aggregate positions credit a 'Bacik augmentation' (sentiment-scored press as a determinant of pathway change). The paper contains no press, news-cycle, social or sentiment data. This is Paul's own extension and should not be cited as Bacik's evidence.

Paul's cycle-model position reads Bacik as showing that lobbying synchronizes with the election cycle and that more money flows in election years. The paper's synchronization claim is about which agencies are targeted (blocks by presidential administration), not about dollars, so do not cite it for a phase coefficient on lobbying spend.

The revolving-door figures (80% of Senators and 60% of Representatives in the main text, versus about 80% and 50% in the SI, with at least one connected lobbyist) are inconsistent within the paper. They are past-employment ties with no dates. Never quote them as access or influence (influence language is barred on revolving-door edges, and D-025 applies).

The paper's networks are unweighted and disregard multi-edges by convention (SI pp. 22-23). That is not an argument for per-edge volume normalization or for dropping regular cosponsorship edges, both of which were REJECTED in this project. Do not cite it that way.

Check staffer_routing.py against D-021. It builds person-to-person hops from co-listing on LDA filings ('co_reported_lobbying_activity' at reported_activity_cost 2, and 'co_reported_firm_association' as a weak opt-in at filing_cost 5). It is unconfirmed whether the reported-activity hop is on by default. If it is, LDA is acting as an edge source.
Preferential attachment is descriptive only. The authors say fitting an evolution model is outside their scope, so it should not seed any weight or prior.
SOPA is one bill, one quarter and 67 public firms. P(IT | SOPA) above 0.4 versus about 0.1 has no strata or uncertainty and should be quoted as a single-case illustration.
Any new analysis here that reuses the paper's g and p functions or its bipartisan index on Melange data stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's markup (217 highlights, no notes) focuses on LobbyView construction, disambiguation, the g and p association functions, registrant types, preferential attachment, election-cycle targeting and the polarization contrast. The parts that bear on the built system agree with it: the system treats LobbyView as an identity source, keeps names decisive over NAICS, keeps in-house and hired-firm spending apart, and borrows only documented definitions for contact inference. The paper's own admission that legislator contact is unobserved strengthens the system's refutation of the lobbied-member link. Paul's cited positions do not record that refutation, so they are stale on that point. Two of Paul's positions over-read the paper. The 'Bacik augmentation' with press sentiment is not in the paper, and the election-cycle synchronization concerns agency targets, not money. His readings for cooperation-v2 and bpf come from the lobbyist bipartisan index, which classifies agents and is not a member-level cooperation trait. The paper does document that the Senate cross-party cosponsorship baseline fell about 40%, which argues for naming the window on bpf.

related.why: This is the original LobbyView database paper. Bacik et al. analyze its successor database.
Kim and Kunisky build bipartite lobbying networks from the same LobbyView and LDA bill links. They give the community-structure counterpart to Bacik's time evolution.
It adds LLM-coded bill positions to LobbyView reports. That fills the position field LD-2 lacks, which Bacik's network also lacks.
It takes the hypergraph and higher-order approach that Bacik defers to future work, applied to the EU lobby network.
Bacik cites it (ref 1) as the survey of empirical lobbying models that the descriptive network work sits beside.
It studies the partisan ties of lobbying firms, which bears on Bacik's finding that lobbying is bipartisan and not polarized.
It covers the PAC channel that Bacik excludes, and finds low overlap between lobbying and PAC spending.
It links donations to lobbying, the step Bacik only mentions. This is relevant to the FEC-LDA bridge.
It mines LDA records for spending patterns using the same disclosure source and faces similar extraction problems.
Bacik cites the access experiment (ref 49) when discussing access. The LDA data cannot observe that access.

paul_entries.citation: Bacik, Karol A, et al. *Measuring the Dynamical Evolution of the United States Lobbying Network*, 6 Feb. 2026.
paul_entries.text:
Bacik, Karol A, et al. *Measuring the Dynamical Evolution of the United States Lobbying Network*, 6 Feb. 2026.

This article by Massachusetts Institute of Technology professors, spearheaded by Professors Karol A. Bacik and In Song Kim, explores the evolution of the congressional lobbying ecosystem, while also presenting a novel database called LobbyView that is highly relevant to the present research and is a fundamental source of data points in models being outlined within the present research. It should be noted that the researchers use case studies to derive empirical observations, such as preferential attachment as a key trait in lobbyists' careers, the role of the upcoming election cycle in terms of who and what is being targeted, and the value of adaptation in response to emerging political events. However, the magnum opus of this article is the data set itself, which can be used to create probabilistic models. These models should be reviewed and dissected to gain a fuller understanding of how they function and can ultimately be augmented. One such route of augmentation is the incorporation of news cycles, social media feeds, and press statements, analyzed via sentiment analysis, as determinants of the likelihood of change within the current pathway and dynamic.
